title: Research Hub: Style & Layout Brief
text:
Design Vision Document A comprehensive guide to the visual identity, layout structure, and user experience for a modern policy-research institute website.



This brief establishes the design direction for a research hub website that communicates credibility, expertise, and modern professionalism. The aesthetic balances academic seriousness with contemporary elegance—approachable enough for media and policymakers, rigorous enough for economists and researchers.
Core Design Principles: - Clarity over complexity - Authority without stuffiness - Timeless elegance, not fleeting trends - Content as the hero

The palette draws from institutional design—think established universities, respected journals, serious think tanks. The Oxford Blue accent conveys trust and intellectual depth without the coldness of pure navy. The warm off-white base prevents the clinical sterility common in academic sites while maintaining professionalism.
Usage Rules: - Accent color appears sparingly: buttons, links, active states, key highlights - Never more than 15% of any given page should be accent-colored - Text always maintains high contrast ratios (WCAG AA minimum)

Visual Treatment:

Background Option A — Subtle Gradient:

Soft gradient from #FAFAF8 (top) to #E8EEF4 (bottom)
Clean, minimal, lets typography breathe

Background Option B — Abstract Geometric:

Faint geometric pattern (interconnected nodes, subtle grid, flowing lines)
8–12% opacity maximum
Suggests networks, data, interconnection without being literal

Background Option C — Photography (if used):

Desaturated, high-contrast architectural or abstract image
Dark overlay gradient (60–70% opacity at text area)
Never stock photos of “business people shaking hands”

When someone lands on this site, they should immediately sense:

Authority — This is a serious institution with serious research
Clarity — The content is accessible, well-organized, easy to navigate
Modernity — Contemporary design sensibility, not a dusty academic relic
Trust — Clean, professional presentation signals credibility
Focus — The research is the star; design supports, never distracts

The design should age gracefully. In 5 years, it should still feel current—because it relies on timeless principles (clarity, whitespace, strong typography) rather than trendy effects.

title: Never-Treated Jackknife Fixes
text:
This document explains the fixes implemented for the Jackknife Figure 2 issues identified on December 2nd. The core problem was that although all counties received a predicted spending value, only ever-treated counties were assigned a value for the binary indicator high. Setting high = 0 for never-treated units

title: Github
text:
Partial replication and extension of Jackson, Johnson, and Persico (2016)


View on GitHub



This repository supports a partial replication and extension of “The Effects of School Spending on Educational and Economic Outcomes: Evidence from School Finance Reforms” by C. Kirabo Jackson, Rucker C. Johnson, and Claudia Persico (2016, QJE). The original study examines how increases in school spending, driven by exogenous timing of court-ordered School Finance Reforms (SFRs), affect long-run educational attainment and adult labor market outcomes, particularly among children from low-income families.
Our work reconstructs the district-level finance panel (F-33 and INDFIN) used in the paper and extends it to county geographies to enable compatibility with proprietary Census data. This involves reprocessing the 1969 GRF (Geographic Reference File) to link school districts with Census tracts and counties, addressing non-tract areas, and implementing aggregation logic for counties with both tract and non-tract zones.



The original JJP (2016) paper and its Online Appendix describe the following key data and methods:
Data Sources:

INDFIN Historical Database (FY 1967,1969–1991) — standardized local government finances including school districts
Common Core of Data (CCD) NCES F-33 Finance Survey (post-1992 annual continuation)
1969–70 School District Geographic Reference File (GRF) for linking Census tracts to pre-reform district geographies

Identification Strategy:

Court-ordered School Finance Reforms (SFRs) serve as exogenous shocks
The number of years of exposure to initial SFR is the treatment variable
Event-study and 2SLS models estimate causal impacts on spending and individual outcomes
Data on court rulings comes from a preceding NBER working paper: https://www.nber.org/papers/w20118

Our Specific Aims:

Develop crosswalks linking F-33 (District) ↔︎ INDFIN (District) ↔︎ Tract (GRF) ↔︎ County (GRF) identifiers
Reconstruct consistent annual per-pupil spending at the county level
Use this data to estimate event studies akin to figure 1 JJP 2016
Extend the analysis with jackknife regressions to identify which counties experienced the largest spending increases from school finance reforms akin to figure 2 in JJP 2016

├── README.md                          # Project documentation
├── CLAUDE.md                          # AI assistant guide
├── run.do                             # Master pipeline runner
└── code/                              # All Stata scripts
    ├── 01_build_district_panel.do     # Build district panels & ID crosswalks
    ├── 02_build_tract_panel.do        # Build tract panel from GRF
    ├── 03_adjust_inflation.do         # Adjust tract spending for inflation
    ├── 04_tag_county_quality.do       # Tag counties as good/bad (baseline data)
    ├── 05_create_county_panel.do      # Interpolate districts & create county panel
    ├── 06_A_county_balanced_figure1.do    # County-level balanced panel Figure 1
    ├── 06_B_district_balanced_figure1.do  # District-level balanced panel Figure 1
    ├── 07_jackknife.do                # Full jackknife analysis
    └── experimental_archive/          # Archived experimental analysis files

Core Pipeline (01-05): Sequential data construction and preparation

01: Build district panels & ID crosswalks
02: Build tract panel from GRF
03: Adjust tract spending for inflation

Coverage:

Time Period: 1967, 1969-2019 (F-33 and INDFIN harmonization)
Geographic Units: 1970 Census tract definitions
Sample Restrictions: Counties with complete baseline data (1967, 1970-1972) for quality analysis

Key Variables:

Spending: pp_exp (nominal), pp_exp_real (2000 dollars), lexp_ma_strict (log spending with 13-year rolling mean)
Population: school_age_pop (used for weighting in aggregation)
Treatment: reform_year (year of court-ordered SFR), relative_year (years since reform)

Counties collapsed from tracts using school-age population weights

Required Software:

Stata (tested with Stata 16+)
Required Stata packages: winsor2, rangestat, eststo/esttab, fred (for CPI data)

Phase I: Data Construction

01_build_district_panel.do - Builds district-year panels from F-33 and INDFIN, creates canonical LEAID ↔︎ GOVID crosswalks
02_build_tract_panel.do - Parses 1969 GRF to link districts to Census tracts, assigns single LEAID per tract
03_adjust_inflation.do - Adjusts tract-level spending for inflation using FRED CPI-U data
04_tag_county_quality.do - Tags counties as “good” or “bad” based on baseline year data completeness (1967, 1970-1972)
05_create_county_panel.do - Interpolates district panel, re-assigns to tracts, imports enrollment data, collapses to county-year panel

Phase II: Main Analysis

06_A_county_balanced_figure1.do - County-level event-study analysis (Figure 1 replication)

Creates balanced panel with complete event windows (-5 to +17 years)
Runs weighted event-study regressions by baseline spending quartile
Produces Figure 1 style plots showing dynamic treatment effects

06_B_district_balanced_figure1.do - District-level event-study analysis (Figure 1 replication)

District-level counterpart to county analysis
Uses district panel instead of county aggregation


Phase III: Jackknife

07_jackknife_heterogeneity.do - Leave-one-state-out jackknife to identify treatment effect heterogeneity

Purpose: Identifies which counties experienced larger spending increases from reforms
Method: For each state, estimates treatment effects excluding that state’s data, then predicts spending increases for excluded state
Panel: Uses balanced panel (complete -5 to +17 event windows)
Outputs:

High vs low predicted spending group comparisons
Quartile analysis showing differential treatment effects



Phase IV: Archived Experiments

experimental_archive/ contains historical robustness checks, alternative specifications, and exploratory analyses




Intermediate Datasets:

districts_panel_canon.dta - District-year panel with quality flags (from 01)
tracts_panel_canon.dta - Tract-year panel with assigned LEAIDs (from 02)
tracts_panel_real.dta - Inflation-adjusted tract panel (from 03)
county_clean.dta - County quality flags (from 04)

Final Analysis Datasets:

interp_d.dta - County-year panel (1967, 1969-2019) with:

Per-pupil spending (nominal and real 2000 dollars)
School-age population weights
Reform exposure variables
Baseline spending quartiles
Quality flags for balanced event-study samples

jjp_interp.dta / jjp_balance.dta - Processed panels for Figure 1 analysis (from 06_A/06_B)
jjp_interp_jk.dta / jjp_balance_jk.dta - Processed panels for jackknife analysis (from 07)
pred_spend_ppe_all_jk.dta - Jackknife predicted spending classifications with:

Predicted spending increase for each county (leave-one-state-out)
High/low treatment group indicators
Quartile classifications
Baseline spending and income quartiles


Analysis Outputs:

Event-study regression estimates
Event-study plots showing dynamic treatment effects
Heterogeneity analysis plots:

High vs low predicted spending group comparisons
Four-quartile differential treatment effects
Combined plots showing treatment effect variation

Jackson, C. K., Johnson, R. C., & Persico, C. (2016). The Effects of School Spending on Educational and Economic Outcomes: Evidence from School Finance Reforms. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 131(1), 157–218.

NCES Common Core of Data: https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/

title: JK Instability
text:
This memo explains why the jackknife plots sometimes show the “high” group dipping below the “low” group. After applying the fixes Nick flagged on Tuesday, the updated charts look cleaner, but the same core issue remains: the jackknife estimates often compress the “high” group and, in several cases, push it below the “low” group.
The main mechanism is straightforward. Some counties that are classified as low in the full-sample prediction model (because predicted spending < 0) flip into the high category when their own state is excluded from the model during the jackknife procedure. This misclassification is likely not the only problem in the jackknife approach, but it appears to be a major contributor to the pattern we observe.
A closer investigation shows that two states — Ohio and Texas — have below-average spending growth among counties that should be in the highest-baseline-spending group. When these states are left out in the jackknife step, their influence disappears, and counties that underperform in the full sample suddenly receive inflated predicted spending values. This pushes them incorrectly into the “high predicted” category.



The goal is simple:

Assign each county a predicted spending change.

Create a binary indicator equal to 1 if predicted spending > 0 and 0 otherwise (for ever-treated counties).

Run an event-study regression using that binary variable.

Under normal circumstances, this should yield the intuitive ordering: high above low.





To keep things simple, consider the specification that controls only for baseline 1971 spending quartile. In the baseline approach, we use the full sample and regress expenditure on quartile indicators. This produces predicted spending values, which we then use to define high (predicted > 0). Running an event-study with this high variable delivers the expected pattern: high consistently exceeds low.








Figure 1: Event study estimates by baseline spending quartile







The jackknife repeats the same regression multiple times, each iteration excluding one state. For each iteration, we:

Re-estimate the model without state s.

Generate predicted spending for counties in the omitted state.

Assign those counties to high/low based on the jackknife prediction.

Move on to the next state.

The advantage is that no single state can dominate the prediction model. The problem is that when we use these jackknife-based predictions to create the high variable for the second-stage event study, we sometimes obtain the reverse ordering: the low group sits above the high group.








Figure 2: Event study estimates by baseline spending and income quartiles



Ordinarily I would assume this pattern reflects a coding mistake, because mechanically the high group should exceed the low group. But after checking the underlying data more closely, that explanation doesn’t hold.
Tabulating pre_q × high (baseline spending quartile × high/low classification) shows the issue clearly:

Finding: 840 counties from pre_q 3 and pre_q 4 (the highest-baseline-spending groups) switch from “low” to “high” under the jackknife. These are units that should theoretically have lower predicted spending changes, not higher.






To understand the flips, we compare the coefficients that form predicted spending in the full sample versus the jackknife runs for Ohio and Texas. Predicted spending equals the main effect plus the quartile adjustment relative to quartile 1 (main + ppe). Here, ppe3 and ppe4 refer to the coefficients on lag_*#pre_q3 and lag_*#pre_q4.


Full Sample - main = 0.0208505
- ppe3 = −0.0227245
- ppe4 = −0.0299217
Ohio Omitted - main = 0.0138311

- ppe4 = −0.0120878
Texas Omitted - main = 0.0248799

- ppe4 = −0.0299885




When Ohio is excluded, ppe4 rises from −0.0299217 to −0.0120878 (+0.0178339).
This boosts quartile-4 predicted spending enough to flip 336 quartile-4 counties into the high group.
When Texas is excluded, ppe3 rises from −0.0227245 to −0.0052331 (~+0.0174914).
This raises quartile-3 predicted spending, flipping 504 quartile-3 counties into the high group.

Together, these shifts generate 840 additional “high predicted” classifications that only appear under the jackknife. This inflates the size of the high group with counties that actually exhibit weak spending growth, which pulls down the average effect for the high group and produces the inversion seen in the jackknife plots.

title: Florida Private School Access and Demographics: 2000 Analysis
text:
This document presents cross-sectional analysis of the relationship between Florida community demographics and private school access for the year 2000. The analysis examines PUMA-level demographic characteristics (income, race, ethnicity, education) and their association with private school exposure measures within a 5-mile radius.
Key Features:

Key Findings
Based on these results:

No Income Sorting on Total Schools: Neither total schools nor religious schools show significant correlation with income. Only non-religious schools are located in higher-income areas.
Racial/Ethnic Patterns: All school exposure measures are positively correlated with Black and Hispanic population shares. Areas with more private schools tend to be more racially diverse.
Education Correlation: Areas with more schools (especially non-religious) have fewer residents with only high school education and more college graduates.
Religious vs. Non-Religious Differences:

Non-religious schools: Associated with higher income, higher Hispanic share, higher college attainment
Religious schools: No income relationship, but associated with racial diversity and lower educational attainment

Multivariate Results: After controlling for demographics, school count has no independent relationship with income. Education (hs_grad) and ethnicity (hisp_share) are the strongest predictors.

title: Florida Private School Access and Demographics: County-Level Analysis
text:
This document presents three parallel analyses of the relationship between county-level demographics and private school access in Florida:

2000 Cross-Section (N=28 counties)
1990 Cross-Section (N=22 counties)
2000-1990 Difference (N=21 matched counties)

Key Features:

Geographic Unit: Counties
Distance Buffer: 5-mile radius (primary specification)
School Levels: Elementary, middle, and high school combined
Weighting: School-age population (ages 5-17) from 1990 Census







Methodology Note



School exposure measures are constructed at the Census block level using geocoded school coordinates, then aggregated to county geography. Demographic measures come from IPUMS Census 5% samples for 1990 and 2000. The difference specification uses 2000 school exposure levels with changes in demographics from 1990 to 2000.

title: Florida Private School Access and Demographics: County-Level Analysis (V2)
text:
This document presents three parallel analyses of the relationship between county-level demographics and private school access in Florida:

2000 Cross-Section (N=21 counties)
1990 Cross-Section (N=22 counties)
2000-1990 Difference (N=21 matched counties)

Key Features:

Geographic Unit: Counties
School Measure: Simple county-level counts (total schools in county)
School Levels: Elementary, middle, and high school combined
Weighting: School-age population (ages 5-17) from 1990 Census







Methodological Change from V1



This analysis uses simple county-level school counts rather than the 5-mile radius buffer approach used in V1. Instead of calculating average school exposure per Census block within a county, we now count the total number of private schools located within each county’s borders. This simplification addresses concerns about the complexity of the radius-based approach and provides a more straightforward interpretation: “How many private schools are in this county?”
The tradeoff is that we lose within-county variation in school access—a family in a rural part of a large county is treated the same as one near a cluster of schools. However, at the county level of analysis, this simpler measure may be more appropriate.

title: Florida Private School Access and Demographics: County-Level Analysis (V2)
text:
Key Findings Summary






Main Results




Cross-sectional patterns: Counties with more private schools have significantly higher Black and Hispanic population shares. This holds for both 1990 and 2000, and for both religious and non-religious schools.
Difference specification: Counties with more private schools experienced larger increases in minority population shares from 1990-2000, and larger decreases in white population share. This is the opposite of a “white flight” narrative.
Interpretation: The positive relationship between private schools and minority shares likely reflects urbanization—growing metropolitan areas have both more demographic diversity and more private schools due to population density. The school-demographic relationship appears to be driven by geography rather than sorting.
Multivariate controls: When controlling for multiple demographics simultaneously, Hispanic share remains a significant positive predictor of school counts in 1990, but most individual predictors become insignificant in the presence of controls, suggesting collinearity among the demographic measures.

title: Florida Private School Access and Demographics: County-Level Analysis (V2)
text:
This document presents three parallel analyses of the relationship between county-level demographics and private school access in Florida:

2000 Cross-Section (N=28 counties)
1990 Cross-Section (N=22 counties)
2000-1990 Difference (N=21 matched counties)
All regression analyses are conducted using the 21 matched counties, while summary statistics are computed using all available counties.

Key Features:

Geographic Unit: Counties
School Measure: Simple county-level counts (total schools in county)
School Levels: Elementary, middle, and high school combined
Weighting: School-age population (ages 5-17) from 1990 Census







Methodological Change from V1



This analysis uses simple county-level school counts rather than the 5-mile radius buffer approach used in V1. Instead of calculating average school exposure per Census block within a county, we now count the total number of private schools located within each county’s borders. This simplification addresses concerns about the complexity of the radius-based approach and provides a more straightforward interpretation: “How many private schools are in this county?”
The tradeoff is that we lose within-county variation in school access—a family in a rural part of a large county is treated the same as one near a cluster of schools. However, at the county level of analysis, this simpler measure may be more appropriate.

title: Florida Private School Access and Demographics: County-Level Analysis (V2)
text:
Key Findings Summary






Main Results




Cross-sectional patterns: Counties with more private schools have significantly higher Black and Hispanic population shares. This holds for both 1990 and 2000, and for both religious and non-religious schools.
Difference specification: Counties with more private schools experienced larger increases in minority population shares from 1990-2000, and larger decreases in white population share. This is the opposite of a “white flight” narrative.
Interpretation: The positive relationship between private schools and minority shares likely reflects urbanization—growing metropolitan areas have both more demographic diversity and more private schools due to population density. The school-demographic relationship appears to be driven by geography rather than sorting.
Multivariate controls: When controlling for multiple demographics simultaneously, Hispanic share remains a significant positive predictor of school counts in 1990, but most individual predictors become insignificant in the presence of controls, suggesting collinearity among the demographic measures.

title: Data Construction Pipeline
text:
Our goal is to replicate Jackson, Johnson, and Persico (2016) as faithfully as possible given our data limitations and some methodological differences. This document details how we constructed the data and replicated the analysis up to the first stage of JJP, which corresponds to their event-study estimates used to construct Figure 1 in the original paper. Replicating JJP required building a complex data pipeline, and we found it essential to document each step to understand exactly which units enter our regressions and why others are excluded.
This document is meant to help readers understand the data pipeline. Those who simply wish to run our code should see the README located in the repository: github.com/maowens-HI/school_finance.


Each stage in the data pipeline corresponds to a distinct Stata do file. At the end of each stage section, you will find a diagram illustrating the data flow and key operations for that stage. A comprehensive diagram showing all stages together appears at the bottom of the document.
Stage 1: District Panel Construction. Historical and modern finance data use different district identifier systems, so we build a crosswalk linking modern (LEAID) and historical (GOVID) identifiers, retaining only clean 1:1 mappings. After appending the panels and linking to Census geography via the GRF, we have 9,428 districts and 424,404 observations. This stage also creates baseline spending flags indicating whether each district has valid data for 1967, 1970, 1971, and/or 1972.
Stage 2: Tract Panel Construction. Assigns each tract to the district serving the largest share of its population. Propagates baseline spending flags using the MIN rule, so a tract is marked as good only if all serving districts have valid baseline data.
Stage 3: County Baseline Spending Tagging. Collapses tract-level baseline spending flags to counties using the MIN function. A county is marked as good only if all of its tracts have complete baseline data. This file is merged into the final analysis dataset so that regressions can exclude counties without good baseline spending.
Stage 4: County Panel Construction. Interpolates small gaps (three years or fewer) in district spending, adjusts for inflation using CPI-U, and collapses to county using school-age population weights. Merges JJP reform treatment data and 1970 Census median family income.
Stage 5: Sample Restrictions and Analysis Variables. Creates spending variables (winsorized per-pupil expenditure [PPE], log PPE, 13-year rolling mean), constructs event-time indicators, and computes baseline spending quartiles within each state. Enforces a balanced panel requirement so that counties must have data for all 23 years of the event window (-5 to +17).
Stage 6: Event-Study Analysis. Runs regressions by baseline spending quartile (Q1–Q4) with county and year fixed effects and clustered standard errors. Produces Figure 1 plots showing spending trajectories before and after reform.



The final analysis sample contains 1,587 counties across 35 states (strict balance on lexp_ma_strict) or 1,986 counties across 43 states (relaxed balance on lexp). See the Sample Attrition section at the end of this document for a full breakdown of sample restrictions at each stage.

text:
1.1 Step 1: Build the LEAID↔︎GOVID Crosswalk
Not every LEAID maps to exactly one GOVID. There are a variety of reasons why this can happen. Districts split, merge, and change codes over time, creating one-to-many and many-to-many relationships. However, there is a conservative solution to this problem: we keep only the clean one-to-one pairs. Concretely, this means building a dataset of only districts where one LEAID corresponds to exactly one GOVID across all years.
Why drop non-one-to-one relationships? Ambiguous mappings prevent us from consistently tracking a district over time. If LEAID “A” maps to both GOVID “X” and GOVID “Y” in different years, we cannot reliably link that district’s historical and modern spending data.
After filtering, we retain 15,047 clean one-to-one pairs in the xwalk_leaid_govid crosswalk.

section: 1.2 Step 2: Add LEAIDs to INDFIN Panel
text:
1.2 Step 2: Add LEAIDs to INDFIN Panel
As stated previously, the INDFIN panel contains historical spending data identified only by GOVID. To link it with modern data and Census geography, we must assign LEAIDs to each GOVID. The first step is to get a list of every GOVID in INDFIN. To do this, we collapse the INDFIN panel by GOVID to create govtag, giving us a file with one row per GOVID. This sets us up to use our crosswalk to assign LEAIDs.
Remember that our crosswalk only contains GOVIDs and LEAIDs with one-to-one relationships. Therefore, we expect a portion of IDs from govtag to go unmatched. The merge attaches quality flags from INDFIN to the crosswalk pairs. After dropping unmatched GOVIDs (those not in the crosswalk), we retain the full 15,047 LEAID-GOVID pairs from the crosswalk. Of these, 13,773 have INDFIN spending data and inherit their quality flags; the remaining 1,274 crosswalk pairs have no INDFIN data, so their flags are set to zero.
govtag                          xwalk_leaid_govid
(GOVID + quality flags)         (LEAID ↔ GOVID)
[MASTER]                        [USING]

     └──────────── MERGE ─────────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
           ┌─────────────────┐
           │ Merge Results:  │
           │ • Master: X     │ ← GOVIDs not in crosswalk (drop)
           │ • Using:  1,274 │ ← Crosswalk pairs not in INDFIN (keep, flags=0)
           │ • Match: 13,773 │ ← GOVIDs matched to LEAIDs (keep)
           └─────────────────┘

1.2.1 Baseline year flags
Before we move on to the next step of our data cleaning process we must first mention another important step concerning the INDFIN panel and govtag. During this part in the pipeline, before we collapse INDFIN into govtag, we create flags indicating whether each GOVID has valid spending in what we call the baseline spending years (1967, 1970, 1971, 1972). The name stems from the fact that we are concerned with the spending of each district during the beginning period of INDFIN, before the exogenous shocks central to our research design occurred.
Baseline spending plays a critical role in our event-study analysis. The event-study design compares how reforms affected districts with different initial spending levels. Districts in the bottom quartile (Q1) had the lowest pre-reform spending; districts in the top quartile (Q4) had the highest. Without baseline spending data, we cannot classify districts into quartiles and cannot test for heterogeneous treatment effects.
If a district lacks valid spending data for the baseline years, we cannot include it in the regression. The quality flags (good_govid_1967, good_govid_1970, etc.) track this. These flags propagate through the pipeline, from districts to tracts to counties, ensuring our final sample contains only observations with complete baseline histories.
This explains why we retain the crosswalk-only pairs from the previous merge. Those pairs have valid LEAIDs, so they can still be linked to census tracts. Their flags propagate through the pipeline like any other observation. But since their flags are set to zero, they will be excluded from analyses requiring baseline spending.

text:
1.3 Step 3: Restrict F-33 Panel to Crosswalk
Steps 2 and 3 are parallel operations on opposite ends of our panel. Step 2 attached LEAIDs to historical INDFIN data (1967–1991); Step 3 restricts modern F-33 data (1992–2022) to the same set of clean identifiers.
Without this restriction, we would include districts that we cannot reliably track across the historical/modern data boundary. For example, if a district’s LEAID maps to multiple GOVIDs, we cannot determine which historical spending record (if any) corresponds to the modern district. By restricting to the crosswalk, we ensure that every district in our final panel has a consistent identifier across all years.
As with the data set in step 2, any observation in the F33 panel whose LEAID does not appear in the crosswalk gets dropped. This leaves us with 15,047 district-year observations, all of which share identifiers with our restricted historical data. The two panels are now ready to be appended into a single district-year panel spanning 1967–2022.

1.4 Step 4: Append Historical and Modern Panels
With both panels now restricted to consistent identifiers, we can combine them. At this point, both panels contain the same identifier variables (LEAID and GOVID), the same spending variable (per-pupil expenditure), and the same quality flags. The panels differ only in their time coverage: INDFIN covers the historical period (1967-1991) and F-33 covers the modern period (1992-2022).

The append confirms our crosswalk worked as intended. The 15,047 unique LEAIDs exactly equals the 15,047 unique GOVIDs: each district has one identifier in each system, no exceptions. Additionally, because INDFIN ends in 1991 and F-33 begins in 1992, there is no year overlap; the append is clean.
Data limitations to note:
The panel is unbalanced: not every district appears in every year due to districts entering or exiting the data over time. Additionally, INDFIN contains no data for 1968 or 1969, creating a gap between 1967 and 1970.

section: 1.5 Step 5: Link to Census Geography (GRF Merge)
text:
1.5 Step 5: Link to Census Geography (GRF Merge)
The final step of Stage 1 connects our district finance data to Census geography. The Geographic Reference File (GRF) from 1969 provides the link between school district boundaries (identified by LEAID) and 1970 Census tracts. This geographic linkage is essential for three reasons.
First, our analysis occurs at the county level. While the original JJP study was at the district level, our replication analyzes spending at the county level. Counties provide a stable geographic unit over time since county boundaries change rarely, and they align well with the administrative data we have access to.
Second, tracts nest cleanly within counties; every tract belongs to exactly one county. By linking districts to tracts, and then tracts to counties in Stage 2, we can compute county-level spending measures through straightforward aggregation.
Third, the GRF provides consistent geographic definitions over time. The 1969 GRF captures district boundaries as of the 1969–70 school year, which means districts that formed later, dissolved earlier, or underwent major reorganization may not appear. We accept this limitation because it mirrors the approach used in JJP and gives us a stable geographic foundation for the entire panel.
With these motivations in mind, we merge the district panel with the GRF on LEAID:
GRF-ID                          dist_panel
(LEAID → tract70)               (LEAID + GOVID + spending)

           │ • Using: 5,611   │ ← Panel obs without GRF match (drop)
           │ • Match: 9,436   │ ← Final canonical panel

                Minor Cleaning

Understanding the merge results
The merge drops a substantial number of observations on both sides, so it’s worth understanding what we’re losing and why.
The 2,932 master-only records represent districts that appear in the GRF but have no finance data in our panel. These districts may have had non-1:1 LEAID-GOVID mappings (and were therefore dropped in Step 1) or may have been small or short-lived districts not consistently tracked in the finance data.
The 5,611 using-only districts are districts from our finance panel that we cannot link to Census geography. This may occur because these districts operated in areas not covered by the 1969 GRF, either because they formed after 1969 or because their boundaries did not contain any tracts in that year’s geographic file.
These dropped observations could potentially be recovered at a later through various means. This may be important if we later determine that the coverage gaps are bias our analysis.

text:
2.2 Key Operations

2.2.1 Step 1: GRF Import and Cleaning
The first step prepares the Geographic Reference File for use. We import the raw GRF, drop special geographies (water bodies, Native lands, ships, tract revisions), and construct standardized identifiers.

Here btc = basic tract code, tsc = tract suffix code, and sdc = school district code.


2.2.2 Understanding Allocated Population
A key variable we create from the GRF is “allocated population.” The raw GRF is at the block/ED level. Each record shows the population of a block/ED (popc) and the percentage of that block/ED served by a given district (perc). Allocated population is the product:
\[
\text{alloc\_pop} = \text{popc} \times \frac{\text{perc}}{100}
\]
We collapse the block/ED-level data to the tract × district level by summing alloc_pop. This gives us the total population in each tract served by each district.

After collapsing by tract × district: District 1 serves 760 people (360 + 400), District 2 serves 240 people. District 1 “wins” because it serves more people, and the tract inherits District 1’s spending data.
Occasionally two or more districts have identical alloc_pop values for the same tract. We need a tiebreaker. The code sorts by LEAID, so the district with the lower LEAID value wins.
Note on sdtc: The school district type code (sdtc) classifies districts by the grade levels they serve: 1 = unified (K-12), 2 = elementary only, 3 = secondary only, 4 = vocational. This classification matters because a single tract may be served by separate elementary and secondary districts. The winner selection actually happens within each district type, so a tract can have up to three assigned districts (one unified, one elementary, one secondary).


2.2.3 Step 2: Tract-District Assignment
Assignment involves three operations.
First, we collapse alloc_pop to the tract × district × type level. This aggregates the block-level data up to tracts while preserving district type distinctions.
Second, we drop vocational districts (sdtc = 4). These are not relevant for K-12 analysis and would complicate the tract assignment.
Third, we pick the winner. For each tract × type combination, we keep only the district with the highest alloc_pop. This means a tract can have up to three assigned districts: one unified (sdtc=1), one elementary (sdtc=2), and one secondary (sdtc=3). In practice, most tracts are served by either a single unified district or by separate elementary and secondary districts.


2.2.4 Propagating Quality Flags
We also need to propagate district-level quality flags to tracts. We use a conservative rule: a tract is “good” for a given baseline year only if ALL districts serving it have valid data for that year. The formula is:
\[
\text{good\_tract\_flag} = \min(\text{good\_govid\_flag})
\]
across all districts in the tract. We create several versions of these flags: year-specific flags (good_tract_1967, good_tract_1970, good_tract_1971, good_tract_1972) and composite flags that combine multiple years (good_tract for all four years, good_tract_6771 for 1967/1970/1971, and good_tract_7072 for 1970/1971/1972). The composite flags are computed at the district level and then propagated to tracts using the same MIN rule.
Why take the minimum? Consider a tract served by three districts: A, B, and C. Even if we assign the tract’s spending to District A (the population winner), Districts B and C also serve students in this tract. If District B lacks 1970 spending data, the tract’s true 1970 spending picture is incomplete; we only observe what District A spent, not what Districts B and C spent. By taking the minimum, we flag such tracts as problematic.
This conservative approach means we may exclude some tracts that would otherwise have usable data. But it ensures that tracts flagged as “good” have unambiguous, complete spending histories.


2.2.5 Step 3: Final Merge
The final step joins district-year spending to tracts. We use joinby LEAID to link the tract-district crosswalk with the district panel from Stage 1. This expands one district-year row into multiple tract-year rows, since the same district can be assigned to multiple tracts. We then merge in the quality flags computed above.
The result is a tract-year panel where each tract has spending data inherited from its assigned district, along with quality flags indicating baseline data completeness.

title: Data Construction Pipeline
text:
3.1 Key Operation: Conservative Collapse
We collapse tract-level quality flags to counties using the minimum. The logic mirrors the tract-level approach: a county is “good” only if ALL its tracts are “good.”
\[
\text{good\_county\_YYYY} = \min(\text{good\_tract\_YYYY})
\]
across all tracts in the county. This produces two types of county quality flags.
Year-specific flags (good_county_YYYY) indicate whether the county has valid spending data for a specific baseline year. For example, good_county_1970 = 1 means every tract in this county has valid 1970 spending data. If even one tract in the county lacks data for that year, the flag equals zero.
Composite flags combine multiple years. The strictest is good_county, which equals 1 only if the county has valid data for all four baseline years (1967, 1970, 1971, and 1972). We also create good_county_6771 (valid for 1967, 1970, and 1971) and good_county_7072 (valid for 1970, 1971, and 1972). These alternatives provide flexibility: a county missing 1967 data but with complete 1970–1972 coverage can still be included in analyses that use a 1971 baseline.
Quality flags propagate through three levels:

District level: good_govid_YYYY = 1 if the district has valid spending data for year YYYY
Tract level: good_tract_YYYY = min(good_govid_YYYY) across all districts serving the tract
County level: good_county_YYYY = min(good_tract_YYYY) across all tracts in the county

At each level, the MIN operation ensures that a single missing observation flags the entire unit as problematic.

section: 4.1 Stage 4.1: District Interpolation and Tract Assignment
text:
4.1 Stage 4.1: District Interpolation and Tract Assignment
Before we can aggregate tracts to counties, we need to address gaps in the district spending data. The district panel contains missing values where spending data was not reported for certain years. This substage fills small gaps using linear interpolation, reassigns districts to tracts, and classifies counties by their tract composition.

4.1.1 Source Datasets
Table 9: Stage 4.1 Data Sources



Dataset
Purpose




dist_panel.dta
District spending (Stage 1)


xwalk_tract_dist.dta
Tract-district crosswalk (Stage 2)


grf_id_tractlevel.dta
Tract metadata with no_tract indicator





4.1.2 Part 1: District Interpolation
The district panel contains gaps where spending data is missing for certain years. We fill gaps of three years or fewer using linear interpolation. Larger gaps risk too much measurement error, so we leave them unfilled.
The process works as follows. First, we compute the gap size between consecutive observations for each district. Second, we flag observations where the next available year is more than three years away. Third, we apply linear interpolation only within the acceptable gap range. This ensures we never extrapolate across long periods of missing data.
Process:

Compute gap size: gap_next = year[_n+1] - year
Flag large gaps: too_far = 1 if gap_next > 3
Interpolate: ipolate pp_exp year if too_far == 0



4.1.3 Part 2: Tract Assignment
After interpolation, we repeat the tract assignment process from Stage 2. We load the tract-district crosswalk, pick the highest-population LEAID per tract, and join the interpolated spending data to tracts. This gives us a tract-year panel with more complete coverage than before interpolation.


4.1.4 Part 3: County Classification
Rural or sparsely populated areas lacked Census tract codes in 1970. The Census Bureau did not define tract boundaries for these “untracted areas,” so the GRF records them differently than tracted areas. We must handle untracted areas carefully to avoid mismeasuring county populations and spending.
We classify counties into four types based on their tract composition.
Type 1 counties are entirely tracted. These are counties where tract boundaries are well-defined. We process them using standard aggregation: sum tract populations and compute weighted average spending.
Type 2 counties contain only a single untracted area. These are counties where the Census defined no tracts. The GRF provides a single “untracted” record for the whole county, and we use county-level population data directly.
Type 3 counties contain multiple untracted areas (two or more). Some counties have multiple distinct “untracted” areas recorded separately in the GRF. This creates ambiguity, since we cannot determine how to distribute county population across these records. We average spending across the untracted units.
Type 4 counties are mixed, containing both tracted and untracted areas. The sum of tract populations does not equal the total county population. We compute the residual population and assign it to the untracted area: untracted_pop = county_total - sum(tract_populations).
With interpolated spending data and county classifications in place, we can proceed to Stage 4.2 to adjust for inflation and aggregate tracts to counties.

text:
4.2 Stage 4.2: Inflation Adjustment and School-Age Population
Stage 4.1 produced a tract panel with interpolated spending in nominal dollars. Stage 4.2 converts spending to constant 2000 dollars, imports school-age population weights, and collapses tracts to counties. The result is a county-year panel with real per-pupil expenditure.

4.2.1 Source Datasets
Table 12: Stage 4.2 Data Sources







Dataset
Purpose




tract_panel_interp.dta
Tract panel from Stage 4.1


enroll_age_tract.csv
NHGIS (National Historical Geographic Information System) tract-level school-age population


enroll_age_county.csv
NHGIS county-level population (for untracted areas)


FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data) CPI-U (Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers)
Inflation adjustment





4.2.2 Step 1: Inflation Adjustment
We convert nominal spending to constant 2000 dollars using the CPI-U (Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers) from FRED. The formula is:
The formula:
\[
\text{pp\_exp\_real} = \text{pp\_exp} \times \frac{\text{CPI}_{2000}}{\text{CPI}_{FY}}
\]
where: - \(\text{pp\_exp}\) = nominal per-pupil expenditure in the given fiscal year - \(\text{CPI}_{2000}\) = CPI-U value for calendar year 2000 (our base year) - \(\text{CPI}_{FY}\) = average CPI-U value for the state’s fiscal year
The adjustment accounts for state-specific fiscal year calendars. School districts report spending by fiscal year, not calendar year, and fiscal year definitions vary by state. Most states use July 1 through June 30, but some use October 1 through September 30 or other calendars. We compute the CPI for each state’s fiscal year as the average CPI across the months in that fiscal year.


4.2.3 Step 2: School-Age Population Import
School-age population (ages 5–17) serves as the weighting variable for county aggregation. We import tract-level population from NHGIS, summing the variables that capture all children ages 5–17 regardless of enrollment status.


4.2.4 Step 3: Handling Tracted vs. Untracted Areas
Untracted areas lack tract-level Census data, so we must handle them separately. We split the data by the no_tract indicator: tracted areas merge with tract-level population data, while untracted areas merge with county-level population data. We then append the two pieces back together.


4.2.5 Step 4: Reshape and Assign Tract-Level PPE (Per-Pupil Expenditure)
Some tracts are served by multiple district types (for example, separate elementary and secondary districts). We reshape the data wide by district type to handle these cases. For tracts with multiple district types, we compute a weighted average based on the proportion of school-age children in each grade range. If data is missing for one district type, we fall back to the available single-district value.
\[
\text{ppe\_tract} = \text{pp\_exp\_real2} \times \text{share\_primary} + \text{pp\_exp\_real3} \times \text{share\_secondary}
\]


4.2.6 Step 5: Handle Mixed Counties
For Type 4 counties (those with both tracted and untracted areas), the sum of tract populations does not equal the county total. We compute the residual population and assign it to the untracted row. This avoids double-counting when we aggregate to counties.
\[
\text{residual\_pop} = \text{county\_total} - \sum(\text{tract\_populations})
\]


4.2.7 Step 6: Collapse to Counties
Finally, we aggregate tract-level spending to counties using a population-weighted average. The weighting ensures that tracts with more school-age children contribute more to the county average.
The formula:
\[
\text{county\_exp} = \frac{\sum_{t \in \text{county}} \text{pp\_exp\_real}_t \times \text{school\_age\_pop}_t}{\sum_{t \in \text{county}} \text{school\_age\_pop}_t}
\]
where: - \(t\) indexes tracts within the county - \(\text{pp\_exp\_real}_t\) = inflation-adjusted per-pupil expenditure for tract \(t\) - \(\text{school\_age\_pop}_t\) = school-age population (ages 5-17) in tract \(t\)
With inflation-adjusted county-level spending in hand, we can now merge the reform treatment data in Stage 4.3.
The Stata command:
collapse (mean) pp_exp_real [w = school_age_pop], by(county year4)
This produces county_exp (weighted average PPE) and school_age_pop (total) for each county-year.

text:
4.3 Stage 4.3: Reform Treatment Data
Stage 4.2 produced a county-year panel with real spending. Stage 4.3 merges school finance reform (SFR) treatment data from Jackson, Johnson, and Persico (2016), hereafter JJP. The reform data identifies when each state’s school finance system was overturned by a court and what type of reform followed. This information is essential for the event-study design, which compares spending trajectories before and after reform.
Source: tabula-tabled2.xlsx (Table D2 from the JJP 2014 NBER Working Paper 20118, extracted via Tabula)

4.3.1 Understanding School Finance Reforms
School finance reforms occur when courts rule that a state’s school funding system violates the state constitution, typically by providing unequal educational opportunities across rich and poor districts. Following such rulings, states implement various reform mechanisms to equalize or increase school funding.
JJP compiled a comprehensive dataset of these court cases and their outcomes. Table D2 (from the 2014 working paper) records the court case name and year, the year the ruling took effect (which may differ from the ruling year), and the reform types implemented after the ruling.


4.3.2 Step 1: Processing the Reform Table
The JJP table contains multiple court cases for some states (if the original ruling was appealed, modified, or followed by additional litigation). We take the first court overturn as the treatment date because:

The initial ruling establishes the legal precedent that forces legislative action.
Later rulings typically build on or modify the initial reform, not replace it.
Using the first ruling provides a consistent definition across states.

The processing involves several steps. First, we import the Excel file. The JJP table is a PDF that we converted to Excel using Tabula. Second, we parse the reform year, extracting the first year the court ruled the system unconstitutional. Third, we keep only the first overturn per state. Fourth, we create reform type flags.
JJP categorizes reforms into five types: minimum foundation plans (MFP), equalization plans (EP), local effort (LE), spending limits (SL), and equity cases (EQ). Reforms are not mutually exclusive. States without court overturns during our study period get reform_year = 0 and never_treated = 1. These states serve as the control group in our event-study design.

4.4 Stage 4.4: Median Income and Output
Stage 4.3 added reform treatment data to the county panel. Stage 4.4 completes the county panel by merging median family income from the 1970 Census. Income serves as an important control variable and helps characterize the economic context of each county at baseline.
The income merge is straightforward. We import the county-level income file, clean the county identifiers to ensure they match our panel, and merge on county name and state FIPS code. The merge is many-to-one since income is measured once (in 1970) but the panel has multiple years per county.
With the county panel complete, Stage 5 applies sample restrictions, constructs event-time variables, and prepares the data for regression analysis.

title: Data Construction Pipeline
text:
5.1 Stage 5.1: Primary Balance
This substage produces the primary analysis dataset with strict balance requirements. The inputs are county_panel.dta from Stage 4.4 and county_qual_flags.dta from Stage 3.

5.1.1 Step 1: Creating Analysis Variables
The first step creates the spending variables we will use in regressions. We construct four versions, each with different properties.
The base variable exp is per-pupil expenditure winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles by year. Winsorizing replaces extreme values with the percentile cutoffs, bounding the influence of outliers without dropping observations. Raw per-pupil expenditure contains extreme values, some from data errors, others from unusual circumstances like a tiny district with very high spending.
From this we compute lexp, the log of winsorized spending. The log transformation enables percentage interpretation: a coefficient of 0.05 means approximately a 5% increase in spending.
We then compute lexp_ma, the log of a 13-year rolling mean. School spending fluctuates year-to-year due to budget cycles, one-time expenditures, and accounting timing. The rolling mean smooths this noise by averaging spending from year \(t-12\) through year \(t\). This choice also mirrors JJP’s use of average spending over ages 5–17.
Finally, lexp_ma_strict is the log of the rolling mean computed only when all 13 years have data. The regular rolling mean uses whatever years are available; the strict version equals missing if any of the 13 years lacks data. This ensures counties with data gaps are excluded rather than measured with error.

Definition

\[
\text{rollingmean}_t = \frac{1}{13} \sum_{j=0}^{12} \text{exp}_{t-j}
\]


5.1.2 Step 2: Event-Time Indicators
Event-study regressions use “event time” (years measured relative to the treatment date) rather than calendar time. We calculate relative year as calendar year minus reform year. For example, if Texas reformed in 1989, then 1987 is relative year -2 (two years before reform), 1989 is relative year 0 (the reform year), and 1995 is relative year 6 (six years after reform). For never-treated states, we set relative year to missing since they have no reform year.
We then create indicator variables for each event-time period. The leads capture pre-reform years: lead_5 equals 1 if relative year is -5 or earlier (binned), lead_4 through lead_1 capture years -4 through -1 individually. The lags capture post-reform years: lag_1 through lag_16 capture years 1 through 16 individually, and lag_17 equals 1 if relative year is 17 or later (binned).
Year 0 (the reform year) is omitted as the reference category. All coefficients therefore measure changes relative to spending in the reform year. A coefficient of 0.10 on lag_5 means spending was 10% higher five years after reform compared to the reform year itself.
Calculating relative year:
\[
\text{relative\_year} = \text{calendar\_year} - \text{reform\_year}
\]

5.1.3 Step 3: Baseline Quartiles
We classify counties by their pre-reform spending levels to test whether reforms affected low-spending and high-spending areas differently. Quartiles are computed within each state using 1971 (fiscal year 1972) data. For each state, we rank counties by their 1971 per-pupil expenditure and divide into four groups: Q1 (lowest 25%), Q2 (25th–50th percentile), Q3 (50th–75th percentile), and Q4 (highest 25%).
Why 1971? We need a baseline year that predates most reforms (most court cases occurred in the late 1970s onward), has good data coverage, and is close enough to reforms to reflect the pre-reform status quo. The year 1971 satisfies all three criteria.
We also compute income quartiles (inc_q) using 1970 Census median family income. This allows us to examine whether reforms helped low-income or high-income areas.


5.1.4 Step 4: Balanced Panel Restriction
The event-study design requires observing each county continuously across the event window. A county that appears and disappears cannot reliably identify treatment effects; changes in spending might reflect the county entering or exiting the data rather than responding to reform.
A county is “balanced” if lexp_ma_strict is non-missing for all 23 years of the event window, from relative year -5 through relative year +17. Why 23 years? The window spans -5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, …, 17, which totals 23 years.
This restriction substantially reduces sample size but ensures clean identification. Counties that fail the balance criterion often have data gaps from missing district-level finance data, from districts that formed or dissolved during the study period, or from incomplete Census tract coverage.
One important caveat: this approach excludes many states with early reforms, since those reforms occur less than 13 years after the first year of available data (fiscal year 1967). The strict rolling mean requires 13 prior years of data, which mechanically excludes early-reforming states from the balanced sample.
\[
\text{balanced} = 1 \iff \text{lexp\_ma\_strict}_{it} \neq \text{missing} \quad \forall t \in [-5, +17]
\]

Some states have very few counties in our final sample, perhaps only 2 or 3. Computing within-state quartiles with so few observations produces unstable estimates. We flag states with sufficient data:

6.1 Regression Specification
The event-study design estimates spending trajectories before and after reform by regressing log per-pupil expenditure on a set of event-time indicators. The model takes the form:
lexp_ma_strict = α + Σ βₖ·lag_k + Σ γₖ·lead_k + δ·year + county_FE + ε

Table 21: Regression Specification Components



Component
Implementation




Outcome
lexp, lexp_ma, or lexp_ma_strict


Fixed effects
County (absorb(county_id)) + Year (i.year)


Clustering
County-level (vce(cluster county_id))


Weights
School-age population ([w=school_age_pop])


Sample
good==1, valid_st_gd==1, reform_year<2000



The outcome variable is the log of the 13-year rolling mean of per-pupil expenditure, though we also estimate specifications using single-year log spending (lexp) and the non-strict rolling mean (lexp_ma). The key regressors are the lead and lag indicators constructed in Stage 5, which capture spending in each year relative to the reform date. Year 0 (the reform year) is omitted as the reference category, so all coefficients measure changes relative to spending in the reform year.
The model includes county fixed effects (absorbed via areg) and year fixed effects. County fixed effects control for time-invariant differences across counties, while year fixed effects control for national trends in school spending that affect all counties equally. Standard errors are clustered at the county level to account for correlation within counties over time. Observations are weighted by school-age population so that larger counties contribute more to the estimates.
The sample restrictions ensure we include only counties with complete baseline data (good==1), in states with at least 10 valid counties (valid_st_gd==1), and with reform dates early enough to observe post-reform outcomes (reform_year<2000).

title: Data Construction Pipeline
text:
Our goal is to replicate Jackson, Johnson, and Persico (2016) as faithfully as possible given our data limitations and some methodological differences. This document details how we constructed the data and replicated the analysis up to the first stage of JJP, which corresponds to their event-study estimates used to construct Figure 1 in the original paper. Replicating JJP required building a complex data pipeline, and we found it essential to document each step to understand exactly which units enter our regressions and why others are excluded.
This document is meant to help readers understand the data pipeline. Those who simply wish to run our code should see the README located in the repository: github.com/maowens-HI/school_finance.


Each stage in the data pipeline corresponds to a distinct Stata do file. At the end of each stage section, you will find a diagram illustrating the data flow and key operations for that stage. A comprehensive diagram showing all stages together appears at the bottom of the document.
Stage 1: District Panel Construction. Historical and modern finance data use different district identifier systems, so we build a crosswalk linking modern (LEAID) and historical (GOVID) identifiers, retaining only clean 1:1 mappings. After appending the panels and linking to Census geography via the GRF, we have 9,428 districts and 424,404 observations. This stage also creates baseline spending flags indicating whether each district has valid data for 1967, 1970, 1971, and/or 1972.
Stage 2: Tract Panel Construction. Assigns each tract to the district serving the largest share of its population. Propagates baseline spending flags using the MIN rule, so a tract is marked as good only if all serving districts have valid baseline data.
Stage 3: County Baseline Spending Tagging. Collapses tract-level baseline spending flags to counties using the MIN function. A county is marked as good only if all of its tracts have complete baseline data. This file is merged into the final analysis dataset so that regressions can exclude counties without good baseline spending.
Stage 4: County Panel Construction. Interpolates small gaps (three years or fewer) in district spending, adjusts for inflation using CPI-U, and collapses to county using school-age population weights. Merges JJP reform treatment data and 1970 Census median family income.
Stage 5: Sample Restrictions and Analysis Variables. Creates spending variables (winsorized per-pupil expenditure [PPE], log PPE, 13-year rolling mean), constructs event-time indicators, and computes baseline spending quartiles within each state. Enforces a balanced panel requirement so that counties must have data for all 23 years of the event window (-5 to +17).
Stage 6: Event-Study Analysis. Runs regressions by baseline spending quartile (Q1–Q4) with county and year fixed effects and clustered standard errors. Produces Figure 1 plots showing spending trajectories before and after reform.



The final analysis sample contains 1,587 counties across 35 states (strict balance on lexp_ma_strict) or 1,986 counties across 43 states (relaxed balance on lexp). See the Sample Attrition section at the end of this document for a full breakdown of sample restrictions at each stage.

title: Data Construction Pipeline
text:
3.2 Why Stage 3 is Separate
Stage 3 produces a standalone file (county_qual_flags.dta) that is merged into the analysis dataset in Stage 5. This separation is intentional: Stage 4 interpolates missing spending data to fill small gaps, but we do not want interpolated values to affect our baseline spending flags or tract/district assignments. By computing the flags before interpolation, we ensure they reflect actual data availability rather than imputed values.
The flags are used in the final regressions to exclude counties without valid baseline spending:

              │  Regressions  │
              │  exclude obs  │
              │  where good   │
              │  flag = 0     │

Summary of Results






Pattern Check



The results match expectations:

Effects monotonically decrease across quartiles
Q4 (richest) counties show small, noisily estimated effects near zero
